channel.title: The Long View
channel.description: A calm five minutes with a big idea, every evening: the thinkers who help us understand how people live together, to read or to listen to.

item.title: The Man Who Went Round the Squirrel
item.description:
It begins with a scene. Some years earlier, James writes, he was with a camping party in the mountains and returned from a solitary ramble to find everyone 'engaged in a ferocious metaphysical dispute'.

Tonight's reading: Pragmatism, Lecture II: What Pragmatism Means, by William James (1906). Read it

Something to think about: The next time you find yourself in a quarrel that seems to have no end, try the man and the squirrel. Ask yourself what practical difference it would make to your life if one side were right rather than the other, and see whether the dispute is really about anything at all.

Read it on the site

item.title: The Long Arc Towards a Gentler World
item.description:
Steven Pinker's 2011 book opens with a claim that sounds like good news: violence in the world has declined on both the short and the long time scales, and the present is probably the most peaceful period in the history of the human species.

Tonight's reading: The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined, by Steven Pinker (2011). Read it

Something to think about: Look back over the past few weeks. Where did you see one of the better angels at work, in yourself or around you? What habit, institution or small act of reason made that moment possible?

Read it on the site

item.title: The Kindness That Defends Itself: Popper's Paradox
item.description:
The paradox of tolerance is a question the philosopher Karl Popper named in his 1945 book The Open Society and Its Enemies. If a free society is genuinely tolerant, must it tolerate those who are not?

Tonight's reading: Paradox of tolerance, by Karl Popper (1945). Read it

Something to think about: Where in your own life do you keep a door open to people or ideas you disagree with, and how do you keep that door from being forced shut from the inside?

Read it on the site

item.title: The Elephant and the Rider: Why Good People Divide
item.description:
Haidt's first and most surprising claim is that our beliefs are driven primarily by intuition, with reason operating mostly to justify what we already feel.

Tonight's reading: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People are Divided by Politics and Religion, by Jonathan Haidt (2012). Read it

Something to think about: Next time you feel very certain about something, notice whether it is your reasoning that speaks first, or your feelings. If your own moral foundations are doing some of the work, what might you be willing to ask of the people who feel just as strongly from a different place?

Read it on the site

item.title: The Bonds That Hold Us: A Week in One Page
item.description:
Monday opened with Lee Harris and his favourite trick: pressing something strange into a familiar shape.

Something to think about: Here is the one question to take into the evening. Think of the group you most feel you belong to, the family, the team, the neighbourhood. What is the bond that actually holds it together, the shared history, the mutual trust, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it? If it were suddenly asked to hold a heavier weight than it was built for, what would you do to help it hold? There is no right answer. You only have to notice the bond, and decide what you would do to keep it strong.

Read it on the site

item.title: What Holds a Society Together: Lee Harris in Ten Minutes
item.description:
Harris starts by being careful with his word. He chose "civilization" because it is value-free, not a banner for us against them.

Tonight's reading: Our new epoch in history: 10 minutes with philosopher/political thinker/novelist Lee Harris, by Bill Steigerwald (interviewing Lee Harris) (2004). Read it

Something to think about: Look at the ties that hold your own community, workplace or circle of friends together. What shared habits, values or trusts make it more than a collection of strangers, and how do you notice when those bonds are quietly wearing thin?

Read it on the site

item.title: The Future Is Not Written: Popper's Open Society
item.description:
Today's reading is Karl Popper's defence of the open society, and it is a natural counterpoint to Lee Harris, because the two are working on the same ground: what happens when a people organise their lives around a story they believe is already written.

Tonight's reading: The Open Society and Its Enemies, by Karl Popper (1945). Read it

Something to think about: If the future really is not written by any law or destiny, what does that ask of the people and the problems in front of you this week? Which small thing, in your own corner, would you be willing to improve, without waiting for a grander plan?

Read it on the site

item.title: The Glue That Holds Civilisation Together: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
item.description:
Long before the phrase 'social cohesion' entered English political vocabulary, an Arab scholar in fourteenth century Tunisia had already given it a name.

Tonight's reading: Asabiyyah, by Ibn Khaldun (1377). Read it

Something to think about: Think about a group you belong to, a family, a community, a team, a generation of friends. What is the thing that actually binds it, the shared history, the mutual obligation, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it together? And what would happen if that bond were suddenly asked to hold a much heavier weight than it was built for?

Read it on the site

item.title: Friend or Enemy: What Makes a People?
item.description:
Schmitt's central claim is memorable for its bluntness: "the specific political distinction … is that between friend and enemy." For him, the political is its own sphere, reducible to none of the others.

Tonight's reading: The Concept of the Political, by Carl Schmitt (1932). Read it

Something to think about: Think of a group you belong to, a neighbourhood, a workplace, a nation. Who or what do its members define themselves against? Does that answer feel natural, or a little unsettling?

Read it on the site

item.title: A Stage, Not a Strategy: Harris on Fantasy Ideology
item.description:
Harris opens with a story that belongs to no single nation or century. When the Spanish ships reached the coast of Mexico, Montezuma had no ready category for white men with steel and strange intentions.

Tonight's reading: Al Qaeda's Fantasy Ideology: War without Clausewitz, by Lee Harris (2002). Read it

Something to think about: Is there a belief you hold, or a cause you once supported, that you would struggle to defend in a calm conversation? What do you think that belief was doing for you, describing the world, or staging it?

Read it on the site
